title: Using the lower back as a bridge (the new lift with your legs)
summary: NH argues the lower back should act as a rigid bridge between the upper body (which holds the bar) and the legs (which move it) in squats and deadlifts. Any lumbar flexion is form breakdown; keeping the spine neutral lets the legs be the limiting factor, prevents overuse injuries and allows him to squat and deadlift heavy twice a week each.
claims: Big legs require more than one lower body day per week, but the lower back is usually what stops people from training legs that often
Proper squat and deadlift technique should be objectively verifiable by eye and by how the body responds afterwards
Lower back pain the day after deadlifting means you either use a style you are not built for or you are not deadlifting properly, regardless of how much you lift
A deadlift is moved with the legs, not the lower back; the lower back only serves as a bridge
In squat and deadlift the limiting factor must be the legs; being limited by low back pain, mobility or rounding shows a technique error
With pristine back squat form, when you fail you simply go back down because only the legs' ability to push failed
'Lift with your legs' is a poor cue because you always lift with your legs; the real problem is under-using the legs and over-using the lower back
Think of body parts in lifts in terms of properties: the legs produce power through flexion while the lower back stays rigid
The lower back connects the upper body that holds the bar with the lower body that moves it, so it takes huge stress and is often damaged
Most people who fail squats or deadlifts with non-bodybuilding form are stopped by excessive lumbar or thoracic rounding, i.e. the lower back failing to stay rigid
Because the lower back must stay rigid, train it to be rigid: its growth should come mainly from isometric stretch, rarely emphasising spinal flexion
The lower back, like the forearms and glutes, gets worked regardless, so it rarely needs dedicated flexion work
Back extensions, reverse hypers and hyperextensions are good lower back work if done as a hip hinge without rounding the lower back
Lumbar flexion under load is a technical flaw, not an inevitable normal occurrence as some fatalistically claim
Keeping the spine neutral through failure greatly improves the ability to grind through sticking points
As a bodybuilder you want to be limited by muscular endurance, not by your structure breaking down
The number one reason people cannot squat and deadlift frequently for years is lower back pain
The lower back sits midway between the two loaded areas, so it carries much of the stress even when kept neutral
Stress that causes muscle fiber damage is good, but stress consuming structural tissue like the spine must be avoided
Letting the low back take over makes it the dominant mover and robs the legs of the tonnage they should get
Any amount of lumbar flexion counts as form breakdown and is wrong for bodybuilders
Since taking his lower body lifts seriously this way about two years ago, he has greatly increased lower body frequency and volume
He deadlifts heavy twice a week and squats heavy twice a week, rotating movements, with always three heavy lower body movements per week, no deloads and no days off, and keeps progressing
Because his lower back stays neutral, it does not suffer overuse injuries; only leg endurance and recovery limit him
The lower back is also a limiting factor for upper back growth
Find a form, technique or stance where the lower back stays neutral and rigid; from start to finish only its angle should change, never its flexion
In the squat, torso angle changes must come from the amount of hip hinge, never from spinal flexion
People who focus on pushing hard with their legs often shoot their hips up on the deadlift and end up lifting with the lower back only
Reversing the squat too quickly makes the hips shoot back and turns it into a good morning
Locking the knees early on a deadlift while the back is still rounded turns the legs into the bridge and makes the lower back the power producer, which is backwards
A good deadlift locks out when hips, knees and shoulders lock at the same time
A correct neutral-back deadlift feels completely different in the hamstrings and core than a poor-form one
Pushing with the legs damages muscle that grows back; hinging with the lower back damages bone and structure that only deteriorates and limits mobility
Everyone without a severe spinal condition can find a technique and lift variation that allows a fully neutral back
Finding a neutral-back technique may cost strength and progression for a while but is worth it long term
exercises: lower back stays rigid bridge; push with legs; hips, knees and shoulders lock together; no lumbar flexion
moved by legs, safe if the back stays neutral
neutral spine; torso angle from hip hinge only; don't reverse too fast
legs should be the limiting factor
hip hinge, don't round the lower back
